sources.title: Royal Ordinances Concerning the Laying Out of New Towns
sources.author: Philip II of Spain, translated by Zelia Nuttall
sources.citation: Zelia Nuttall, 'Royal Ordinances Concerning the Laying Out of New Towns,' The Hispanic American Historical Review, Vol. 4, No. 4 (1921), pp. 743-753. Internet Archive.
sources.context: Ordinances 111-122 from the town-planning decree of Philip II, issued in 1573 and translated by Zelia Nuttall in 1921. They set out how a new Spanish town in the Americas was to be sited and laid out.
questions: What qualities does the ordinance say to look for in a town site, and what is the site to avoid?
Where is the main plaza placed in a coastal town, and where in an inland town?
Which activities are pushed to the edge of the plan, and for what reason?
These ordinances were issued for new towns in the Americas. Who is doing the planning, and who is not mentioned?

sources.title: Manchester: the separation of the classes
sources.author: Friedrich Engels
sources.citation: Friedrich Engels, The Condition of the Working-Class in England in 1844, translated by Florence Kelley Wischnewetzky (London: Swan Sonnenschein, 1892), Chapter 5. Project Gutenberg eBook 17306.
sources.context: From Chapter 5 of Engels's study of the English working class, based on his time in Manchester. He describes how the commercial core, the workers' districts, and the middle-class suburbs were arranged.
questions: How does Engels say the working-people's quarters are kept apart from the rest of Manchester?
What occupies the centre of Manchester, and what is it like at night?
Where do the wealthy live, and how does Engels describe their route to business?
Engels wrote as a mill owner's son who knew the city well. What might that lead him to stress?

sources.title: Baghdad under the Abbasids
sources.author: Yakut (Yaqut al-Hamawi), in an English anthology
sources.citation: William Stearns Davis, ed., Readings in Ancient History: Illustrative Extracts from the Sources, Vol. II: Rome and the West (Boston: Allyn and Bacon, 1912-13), pp. 365-367. Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Fordham University.
sources.context: A description of Baghdad at the height of the Abbasid caliphate, compiled as a geographical dictionary and printed in an English source anthology of 1912. It presents the city at its most prosperous.
questions: How does the account describe the shape of Baghdad and its quarters?
What does it claim about water, sweeping, and lighting?
The account gives the population as 'over two millions'. What should make a reader cautious about that figure?
This text reached English readers through a 1912 anthology. What kind of source is it, and what can it not tell us?

interpretations.work: The Growth of the City: An Introduction to a Research Project
interpretations.claim: Burgess argued that a city grows outward from its centre in a series of concentric zones, beginning with the central business district and passing through a zone of transition and workers' housing to a commuter zone, as each ring is invaded by the one inside it.
interpretations.note: The model was drawn from Chicago in the 1920s. Hoyt's sector model (1939) and Harris and Ullman's multiple-nuclei model (1945) both challenged the ring pattern, and later geographers showed that it fits few cities outside North America.

interpretations.work: The Global City: New York, London, Tokyo
interpretations.claim: Sassen argued that a handful of cities became the command points of a dispersed world economy, concentrating finance and the specialized producer services that support it, and producing a sharper split between high-paid professionals and low-paid service workers.
interpretations.note: Critics say the idea imposes a single hierarchy on very different cities, overstates the break with earlier port and industrial cities, and neglects cities that command regions rather than the whole economy. The ranking of world cities remains contested.

choices: Its position in relation to the surrounding region and routes
The exact ground it stands on
activities.feedback: Site is the ground itself - slope, water, defensibility; situation is where that ground sits in a wider region of routes and resources.

activities.prompt: Why did many cities grow along a river's fall line?
choices: Boats stopped and water power began where rivers left hard rock for the coastal plain
The soil there was always the most fertile
The rivers were too shallow to cross
activities.feedback: A fall line is a break-of-bulk point: goods changed from boats to roads or rail, and mills used the drop in the river.

activities.prompt: Burgess's concentric-zone model placed which area at the centre?
choices: The central business district, which he called the Loop
activities.feedback: Burgess saw growth as expansion outward from the central business district, with each ring invaded by the next.

activities.prompt: What did Hoyt's sector model add to Burgess's rings?
choices: Residential growth in wedges along transport routes and high ground
That all land uses are mixed together
activities.feedback: Hoyt studied 142 American cities and found high-rent districts pushing outward in sectors rather than rings.

choices: A flat plain with an evenly spread population and equal transport in all directions
A mountainous coast with uneven settlement
activities.feedback: The hexagons are a logical result of the assumptions; real terrain, uneven population, and history bend the pattern.

activities.prompt: The Ordinances of Philip II in 1573 required a new colonial town to have...
choices: A rectangular central plaza with the church and council house on it
A separate quarter for each religion
activities.feedback: The grid and the plaza came first; slaughterhouses, tanneries, and fisheries were sent where their filth could be carried away.

activities.prompt: In the medina of Fez or Cairo, the core of the city was...
choices: The Friday mosque and the market, with houses facing inward to courtyards
activities.feedback: Houses turn their backs to the street and face an inner courtyard, and the plan has no European-style central square.

choices: Grading neighbourhoods and refusing mortgages and insurance to Black and immigrant districts
Drawing city boundaries in red ink
activities.feedback: The Home Owners' Loan Corporation's security maps helped fix a racial geography of investment that outlasted the maps.

activities.prompt: Sassen's 'global city' thesis holds that a few cities...
choices: Became command points for finance and producer services in a dispersed economy
activities.feedback: For Sassen the key is command and coordination rather than size, and the thesis is contested.

activities.prompt: The Ordinances of 1573 and Engels describe two ways of ordering a city. Compare what each assumes about where different people and activities belong, and what each leaves out.
activities.context: Ordinances of 1573: 'The main plaza whence a beginning is to be made, if the town is situated on the seacoast, should be made at the landing place of the port. If the town lies inland, the main plaza should be in the middle of the town.' - Engels, 1845: 'The town itself is peculiarly built, so that a person may live in it for years, and go in and out daily without coming into contact with a working-people's quarter or even with workers.'
rubric: states what each text assumes about where people and activities belong
uses a specific detail from each text
